```{r}
# Assuming all relevant variables are numeric

heatmap(corr_matrix, main="Correlation Matrix Heatmap", Colv=NA, Rowv=NA, scale="none", 
        col=colorRampPalette(c("blue", "white", "red"))(200))
```

```{r}
# a more aesthetically pleasing heatmap
library(ggplot2)
library(reshape2)

# Melt the correlation matrix
melted_corr_matrix <- melt(corr_matrix)

# Plot using ggplot2
ggplot(melted_corr_matrix, aes(Var1, Var2, fill=value)) +
    geom_tile() +
    scale_fill_gradient2(low="blue", high="red", mid="white", midpoint=0, limit=c(-1,1)) +
    theme_minimal() +
    labs(title="Correlation Matrix Heatmap", x="", y="") +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))


```

```{r}

# Load the library
library(caret)

# Assuming 'df' is your dataframe
# Prepare the data
X <- data[, !(names(data) %in% 'LUNG_CANCER')]  # Drop the 'LUNG_CANCER' column
y <- data$LUNG_CANCER  # Target variable

# Split the data into training and testing sets
set.seed(10)  # Set seed for reproducibility
trainIndex <- createDataPartition(y, p = 0.8, list = FALSE)  # 80% for training
X_train <- X[trainIndex, ]
X_test <- X[-trainIndex, ]
y_train <- y[trainIndex]
y_test <- y[-trainIndex]



```


```{r}
# Print the dimensions of the training and testing datasets
print(dim(X_train))
print(dim(X_test))
print(length(y_train))
print(length(y_test))

```


# LOGISTIC MODEL:

Formula:
The logistic regression model predicts the probability that a given input point belongs to the category marked as "1" (as opposed to "0"). The formula for logistic regression is based on the logistic function, which is defined as:
$$
P(Y=1 \mid X)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}
$$

Here:
- $P(Y=1 \mid X)$ is the probability that the dependent variable $Y$ is 1 given the predictors $X$.
- $e$ is the base of natural logarithm.
- $z$ is a linear combination of the predictor variables, expressed as:
$$
z=\beta_0+\beta_1 X_1+\beta_2 X_2+\cdots+\beta_n X_n
$$


Components:
- $\beta_0, \beta_1, \ldots, \beta_n$ are the coefficients of the model. $\beta_0$ is the intercept, and $\beta_1, \ldots, \beta_n$ are the coefficients of the predictor variables $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$.
- $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ are the predictor variables.



Decision Rule:
- To make a prediction, logistic regression uses a decision rule. If $P(Y=1 \mid X)$ is greater than a certain threshold (commonly 0.5 ), the outcome is classified as 1 ; otherwise, it is classified as 0.




Estimating Parameters:
- The parameters $\beta$ of the model are usually estimated using maximum likelihood estimation (MLE). This method seeks to maximize the likelihood function, which measures how probable it is to observe the given set of data, under the model parameters.

Advantages:
- Logistic regression is simple and computationally efficient.
- It provides probabilities for outcomes, which can be useful for understanding the confidence of predictions.
- It can be regularized to avoid overfitting.

Limitations:
- Assumes linear relationship between the log odds of the dependent and independent variables.
- Not suitable for more complex relationships or non-linear data patterns without transformation or additional techniques.



```{r}
library(ROCR)

```

```{r}
model1 <- glm(y_train ~ ., data = X_train, family = binomial)
y_pred1 <- predict(model1, newdata = X_test, type = "response")

# Create a prediction object
pred <- prediction(y_pred1, y_test)


```

```{r}
# Calculate performance for ROC
perf <- performance(pred, "tpr", "fpr")
perf_df <- data.frame(
  False_Positive_Rate = perf@x.values[[1]],
  True_Positive_Rate = perf@y.values[[1]]
)


# Calculate AUC
auc <- performance(pred, "auc")
auc_value <- auc@y.values[[1]]

print(auc_value)
```


```{r}
# Create ROC curve using ggplot2
ggplot(perf_df, aes(x = False_Positive_Rate, y = True_Positive_Rate)) +
  geom_line(color = "#3498db", size = 1.5) +  # Change to a brighter blue
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", color = "#bdc3c7", size = 1) +  # Softer gray for the diagonal
  geom_area(aes(y = True_Positive_Rate), fill = "#ecf0f1", alpha = 0.5) +  # Add area under curve
  geom_point(aes(x = False_Positive_Rate, y = True_Positive_Rate), 
             color = "#e74c3c", size = 2) +  # Add points
  labs(title = "ROC Curve", 
       subtitle = sprintf("Area Under Curve (AUC) = %.4f", auc_value),
       x = "False Positive Rate", y = "True Positive Rate") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold", color = "#34495e"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 14, face = "italic", color = "#34495e"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 14, color = "#34495e"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 12, color = "#34495e"),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.title = element_blank()
  )
```
